content.thinking:
I'll write the whole module carefully in one pass to avoid crash risk, designing a Genshin-style red panda perched on a mossy stone with toon cel-shading, glowing elemental motifs, and gold filigree details, scaling proportions realistically against the stone's height.

For the pose, I'll keep it simple and stable: the panda stands on all fours on the rounded boulder with legs spread for balance, tail arched up behind it in an S-curve rather than attempting a risky lifted-paw stance. I'm planning the coordinate system and bone hierarchy next, with the root joint at the panda's hips and the stone attached as its own part.

I'm working out the stone's shape and height now—scaling a flattened icosahedron so its top sits around 0.30-0.34 units high, keeping its base barely sunk into the floor, while making sure the panda's overall height (including the arched tail) still fits proportionally.

Switching to a sphere with flat shading so the poles touch the floor properly, centered at y=0.15 with scale giving a bottom near -0.01 and top near 0.31. Now I'm calculating the stone's curved surface height under the panda's feet, since the ellipsoid top is rounded and each paw position will sit at a slightly different elevation depending on its offset from center.

Checking the math, feet bottoms land around y≈0.32, sunk slightly into the moss cushion so the grass tufts can hide the contact point. Now I'm moving on to the panda's proportions, going for a stylized cute look with a bigger head and tail.

I'm setting up the body's spine chain running from hips to chest to shoulders, checking belly clearance above the feet so the short legs and low-slung posture read correctly, then continuing the chain up toward the neck.

Now I'm placing the head, sizing its width for the characteristic wide red panda face, and setting the overall height including ears. I'm also sketching the tail as a curling S-shaped path arching up and forward from the hips, balancing its large size against the head so the proportions still feel right.

Adding tail ring striping logic...

Now I'm working out a Genshin-style bright palette: vibrant rust-orange for the coat, darker burnt orange for the back, a deep plum-brown for the belly and legs, and cream for face markings, plus considering a cyan/teal iris for striking contrast against the warm fur tones.

I'm also settling on the gold, moss-green, and lavender-grey stone accents, and leaning toward a Dendro theme with subtle glowing green motifs—maybe a few glowing runes or small mushroom-like accents on the stone—kept minimal so the design stays clean.

For the panda itself, I'm adding Genshin-style gold filigree: a small collar with a tassel and green gem pendant, gold ear-cuffs, and a gold tail ring with tassel.

Now I'm planning the bone structure, starting with the hips as root and building a spine chain upward toward the chest.

Then I'll add a neck chain parented to the spine's end, followed by a head joint attached at the neck's tip. For the body skin itself, I'm planning a loft across stations tied to the bone chain from hips through spine.

Since hips and spine1 share nearly the same t value, the dedup logic drops the earlier one and keeps spine1, so hips ends up owning nothing while spine1 covers the stretch before it — that's fine since the root joint doesn't need its own mesh. I'm now reconsidering the approach: maybe simplify by lofting the body with just the spine chain as the bone, then handling the neck as a separate overlapping sweep to avoid a visible seam.

For the fur, I'm leaning toward fur cards with simple two-tone SVG tuft textures rather than full fur simulation, placing them at cheeks, tail tip, chest, ears, and leg backs — batched per texture so the part count stays well under limits. I also want the belly fur edge to use a zigzag toon paint for a cel-shaded look.

Now I'm working out the countershading: rusty back and flanks against darker, plum-brown underparts and legs, using position-based fur-edge gradients along different axes (height for the torso belly, a different axis for the limbs) so the color transitions feel like natural fur boundaries rather than flat gradients.

I could nest a mottle blend of rust tones for the fur edge, which still works as a paint. Now let me move to the head, the hero piece — placing the head joint around [0, 0.60, 0.33] aimed slightly forward and down, and thinking through the cream face markings carefully.

I'm sketching out the head geometry: a broad rounded cranium sphere, cheek ruff spheres with outward cream tufts, a short cream muzzle with a dark plum nose tip, and I'm starting on the lower jaw next.

For the mouth and eyes, I'm planning a small cream jaw piece positioned below the muzzle, then working out where to place anime-style eye decals on the skull sphere -- figuring out the azimuth and elevation angles so the eyes sit symmetrically with the characteristic red panda dark tear-mark lines running toward the mouth.

I'm also checking for overlap between the eye decals and the forward-projecting muzzle sphere, since the muzzle extends far enough in z and y that it could clip into the lower edge of the eyes, so I need to nudge the eye position or muzzle size to avoid that collision.

Minor overlap at the lower inner edge is acceptable. For the mirrored decals, I'm working out that azimuth 90 corresponds to +X, so setting s=+1 maps correctly to the creature's left eye with mirror applied when s>0, matching the kit's convention.

Since I'm unsure whether an explicit `dir` overrides the normal set by a Hit, I'm leaning toward passing `at: hit` with an explicit `dir` tilted slightly toward the side (using s to flip direction) so the eye decal reads naturally on the curved surface, though I'd ideally confirm this behavior by checking the decal source.

Now I'm thinking about the facial markings: adding small cream eyebrow-like spots above the eyes, and painting the head so the cream covers the muzzle, cheeks, and eye region while a rust-colored cap covers the forehead, using position-based rules relative to the head center to decide where each color applies.

Writing paint function...

Still writing coloring logic...

I'll skip the forehead blaze detail and keep the markings simple with a zigzag pattern, since I can't actually render this to verify. I should focus on writing robust code without unused imports or type errors, then carefully build out each section using the correct APIs.

Setting up imports and body layout constants...

Actually, having hips and spine1 at identical positions worries me — that creates a zero-length bone, which could cause NaN issues in nearest-bone weight computations. I'll separate them: put hips slightly behind at [0,0.49,-0.22] and start the spine chain at [0,0.50,-0.14], giving the hips bone actual length.

The hind legs and tail will both parent off hips, and the spine continues upward through a few more joints. I'm also laying out the body loft stations from rump to end, defining width and height at each point along the spine to shape the torso silhouette.

I should nudge the body up slightly since the legs come out a bit short for stylized proportions, and I'm checking how the hips joint and spine1 share ownership in the loft blend based on their position along the spine curve.

Now I'm working out how the neck chain attaches to the spine, confirming the parent-child link and that the neck path's starting point lines up cleanly with where spine3's bone span ends.

For the head, I'm placing its joint at the neck chain's endpoint and figuring out the direction vector so the head bone aims correctly in local space, roughly pointing forward and slightly upward to match where the head center should sit.

I'm sweeping a thick neck tube with tapered radius, colored in the coat's rust tone, since red pandas have fairly substantial necks connecting directly to the head. Then I'm adding a jaw joint parented to the head, positioned slightly below and forward, and building the skull as a scaled sphere geometry parented to the head bone.

Now I'm working out the ears -- rounded triangular shapes, cream inside with rust outside and a white rim, built from flattened spheres oriented to point up, outward, and slightly forward from the top-sides of the head, with tilt and roll angles to get that characteristic red panda ear splay.

Still arranging ear tufts...

To be safe, I'll just explicitly pass the bone option on the card to pin it to the head, since the nearest-joint fallback is ambiguous near the ear. I'll skip using ring here since its default radius and joint behavior could cause issues.

Instead I'll compute tuft positions manually with trig, deriving each point from the ear center using cosine/sine offsets along right/up vectors, and feed those into frame() calls bound to the head bone. I'll write a small helper, tuftsAround, to generate these frames, and design the tuft texture as a simple two-tone fur shape tinted by color, with separate cream and shadow-toned variants.

Still writing SVG code...

Next I'm sketching the red panda's leg design — short limbs in a dark plum tone with distinct dark paw pads, possibly cream accents.

For a plantigrade hind leg, I'm working out a 3-segment setup with the final segment flat along the sole direction so the foot rests naturally on the floor, adjusting the bend count since the sole constraint removes a degree of freedom.

I'm placing the hip, ankle, and toe coordinates to check that the leg length can actually reach the target foot position while keeping the sole flat on the ground, computing the hip-to-ankle distance to verify reachability.

With a 0.126 hip-to-ankle span, the triangle law of cosines shows the knee bulges forward about 8cm, which seems reasonable for a crouched hind-leg pose.

Checking where that puts the knee relative to the body ellipse, it actually lands mostly buried inside the belly contour — which makes sense since red pandas' thighs are essentially fused against the torso, leaving only the lower leg visibly protruding.

I'm reconsidering the limb lengths to keep the leg straighter, trying shorter segments like [0.12, 0.11, 0.07] and checking root-to-ankle distances against the total segment length to confirm the geometry is feasible. I'm also second-guessing how the limb solver handles the "sole" parameter — the docs sample seems to pass one more bend direction than the stated rule of "one fewer direction with sole" would suggest, so I need to figure out the actual bend-count convention before trusting my own calls.

Working out hip, knee, ankle and toe coordinates for the hind leg, then checking the segment lengths between hip-knee and knee-ankle to make sure they're reasonable.

The knee-forward, ankle-back arrangement actually matches the typical digitigrade bend seen in cat-like hind legs, so I'll keep it and just nudge the heel height down slightly for a more natural red panda stance, then set the thigh and shin radii.

Now I'm plotting the foreleg joints from shoulder to toe tip, placing the elbow slightly back for a natural bend, and assigning tapering radii down the limb. I'm also adding a flattened paw shape at the wrist to suggest a paw pad.

Checking the foot sinks slightly into the moss cushion, letting the paw bottom settle just below the cushion's top surface so it looks naturally grounded rather than floating.

Checking the other footprint points, the toe and heel positions both land near y=0.318-0.323 against the cushion surface, which works out well. I'll settle on paw bottoms at roughly y=0.318, setting F=0.325 with paw centers at F+0.015 and ry=0.022.

Now I'm reconsidering the stone's proportions -- a smaller, rounder rock feels more fitting for a balancing pose than a wide base, so I'm shrinking the main body to [0.36, 0.165, 0.33] with a cushion of [0.30, 0.04, 0.29] on top, checking that the cushion's footprint still aligns with the paw placements at the edges.

Still, the cushion overhangs the stone's narrower top too much, giving a mushroom-cap look rather than a natural mossy boulder. I'm switching to a lathe-profile boulder with a wide flat top instead, defining the outline as a series of radius/height points to get a believable rounded shape.

I'll attach the lathe to the hips bone, then build a separate lathe for the moss cap draping over the top of the stone with a gently tapering outline.

I verify the outer and inner moss boundary points don't cross each other at matching x-values, confirming the moss patch outline stays geometrically valid along the stone's curve.

I'm working out the radial distances for each foot's position to determine where it sinks into the moss surface, building a helper function that interpolates the moss height from the outline points and applies a small sink depth for each paw contact point.

The lathe's coarse segment count will slightly flatten the radius between vertices, lowering the moss top a few millimeters, which is fine. To break up the perfect radial symmetry, I'm adding faceted rock clumps around the base using low-poly spheres with flat shading, partially embedded and painted stone-colored, with some moss caps scattered on top for irregularity.

Now I'm defining the paint logic for the rock surfaces: combining a mottled moss paint for upward-facing areas with noise-driven thresholds, and a patchy stone paint with warmer base tones for the rest, wrapped in a cel shader for the stylized look.

Then I'm adding crack detail using cell/Voronoi noise to pick out thin dark lines where cell boundaries are close, and layering moss cap shading on top. For vegetation, I'm scattering grass tuft cards across the mossy top surface, filtering by upward-facing normals and controlling density, size, and lean of each blade.

I'm giving the grass cards a flow direction so they bend consistently rather than random, letting some tufts spill near the panda's paws for a natural touch, and considering a drape of hanging moss around the rim edge.

I'm scattering hanging moss tufts along the rim using explicit frame positions with lean angles for a vine-like drape, then planning a few small glowing Dendro-style flowers made from flattened petal spheres plus a center sphere, tinted green-lime to match the moss theme.

Now I'm thinking through a glowing Dendro leaf emblem glyph decal on the stone's front face, using glow applied to a decal texture so the elemental rune glows against the lathe-curved surface.

Now I'm thinking through the gold filigree accessories for the figure—planning a collar necklace at the neck with a cyan gem pendant and tassel, considering using a torus ring aligned to the neck axis to form the collar loop.

Bumping ring radius slightly to 0.088 to clear the neck mesh, checking the ring doesn't clash with the head's cheek ruff or chest geometry at that z-position — looks fine. Now positioning the pendant at the front-bottom of the collar ring.

Writing pendant and tassel geometry...

Now I'm thinking about smaller accessories: a gold ring around the ear with a tiny dangling teardrop earring, and a gold band wrapped around the tail.

I'm also planning front leg gold bangles and a decorative gold leaf-shaped hairpin with a gem sitting between the ears like a small crown ornament.

Working out the extrusion geometry and outline points for that fan-shaped crest...

Computing the surface tangent direction for the upward lean orientation at that elevation...

I'll define a headPoint helper computing ellipsoid surface points from azimuth/elevation with a lift parameter, plus a normal direction derived from the ellipsoid gradient. Then I'll plan smaller features: a glowing octahedron forehead gem, teal irises, cream brow spots, and a dark plum nose placed near the muzzle front, keeping the flat color palette under 64 colors.

For the mouth, I'm positioning the muzzle and jaw spheres so they overlap slightly to read as a closed mouth with the cream jaw showing as a chin, then adding thin ink rods from the nose down through the philtrum and curving outward on each side to form the mouth line.

Now I'm adding whiskers as a set of tiny cream-colored rods extending from the cheeks, keeping them very thin with low sides for subtlety.

For the nose I'm sticking on a tiny white sphere highlight, and for the cheeks I'm scattering cream tuft cards outward and back using surface scatter with a fixed lean and flow direction. I'm positioning the cheek spheres symmetrically with cream cel paint, but checking they don't clash with the eye decal placement nearby.

I'm computing whether the cheek sphere geometry actually pokes through the skull surface near the eye decal location by comparing z-depths at matching x/y coordinates, since decals sit just barely off the skull and any cheek bulge could poke over them.

Confirming the cheek stays just inside the skull surface there, so it's safely hidden and the decal placement works fine. Moving on to body markings now—thinking through the red panda's coloring for the back and considering whether to add a darker rust saddle stripe along the midline while keeping the cel-shaded fur gradient between rust and plum tones.

I'm reconsidering the mottling for the fur texture since high contrast looks too murky, so I'll soften it, and I'm planning fur card tufts along the belly and chest edges. Since real red pandas have dark bellies rather than cream, I'm shifting the chest/legs to a deep plum and keeping cream reserved for the face, with the back staying rust.

Now I'm working out the tail design—alternating rust and dark rust bands with a darker plum tip—using a banding function based on position along the tail to assign colors per ring, roughly eight bands with a distinct tip segment.

I'm refining the ring boundaries to zigzag around the tail's circumference instead of forming straight bands, tying the pattern to both position along the tail and angle around it. I'm also setting up the tail as a chain of five segments with a tapering fluffy radius profile and a rounded tip, then thinking through how to scatter fur tufts along it oriented toward the tip using a sweep-based frame since there's no direct tangent vector available per hit.

I'll alternate textures by ring parity, grouping cards into separate calls per ring (rust, deep, tip), keeping the total count moderate around 600. The sweep angles spread widely around the tail with some lean applied to each card.

Now I'm thinking through the ears with a gold earring detail, and planning to structure the build as helper functions inside a closure. For the dorsal fur, instead of defining separate colored sectors, I'll paint a stripe directly within the coat layer wherever the position is near the centerline and the normal points upward.

Writing custom paint function for coat...

Thinking about the red panda's fur coloring: chin and chest area need a cream bib transitioning to rust, versus the actual dark chest red pandas have — deciding whether to stylize this with a cream bib based on vertical position on the neck/body.

For leg shading, I'm defining a position-based paint function that switches between rust and plum colors depending on height, using zigzag noise to create a natural-looking boundary near the hips and shoulders, while keeping paws a darker purple-black tone without toe details.

Setting up imports and metadata for the file, then defining the color palette constants for rust, cream, plum, gold, teal, and leaf tones...

Writing texture generation code...

Still drawing grass blade paths...

For the moss and tassel, I'm reusing the grass texture for hanging moss, then sketching a tassel with a gold bead cap at top and fanning strands below in gold, teal, and white to match the Genshin style.

Still writing SVG code...

With the leaf decal shape finished, I'm moving to the body-building code, starting a builder function with a seeded RNG and defining the hip joints.

Writing joint hierarchy...

Jaw bone extends from head joint to jaw joint, with meshes assigned to whichever bone has the most weight nearby. Now I'm defining leg geometry, starting with a moss height function and the outer profile points for the moss top.

Checking parent attachment: shoulder parented to spine joint 2 since it falls within the spine3 span, while hind legs parent to hips. I'm also verifying the shoulder's x-position stays within the body flank, with the elbow positioned slightly wider under the belly.

Now I'm working out the leg sweep geometry, using decreasing radii along the chain toward the toe with rounded caps, then adding the paw as a scaled sphere attached to the chain's tip joint—though I need to figure out whether to reference the tip property directly or index into the joints array, and recount how many joints a 4-name chain actually produces.

For the paws themselves, I'm placing the front paw between wrist and toe and the hind paw between heel and toe, each with slightly different scale and z-range to fit the leg shape. Then I'm planning small toe spheres and claw spikes at the front of each paw, multiplied across all four feet for the full set of details.

Now I'm shaping the toes as subtle bumps with small spheres, and adding claw spikes projecting forward from each toe tip with a cream color. I'm also setting up a gold bangle ring around the front wrists, aligning its torus shape along the leg direction with a radius sized to fit snugly.

I'm skipping the rear anklets and extra hind toe details, then moving to the body and neck geometry—building a loft for the torso through multiple stations with varying radii, and a tapered neck sweep with its own paint coloring.

Checking the neck-to-skull fit confirms the radii and positions line up correctly, and the head sits just above the shoulders with a plausible neckless red panda silhouette. With the skull and cheeks confirmed, I move on to adding whisker rods and start placing the nose.

Now I'm placing the nose as a small plum sphere with a tiny white highlight stuck on top, then setting up the ear-building loop with outward/up/forward facing directions, outer and inner ear spheres, and rim tufts for each side -- working through how the sphere's local axes align to aim the ears correctly in world space.

I'm checking the math for ear placement against the skull curvature to confirm the ear base sits embedded and visible, then deciding on the ear colors -- going with a darker rust/plum tone for the outer ear to mimic a red panda's dark ear backs against the cream inner fur.

I'm computing tuft positions along the ear rim using angular offsets and axis vectors to scatter small fluff cards around the top edge.

For the card frames, I'm computing the outward direction as a blend of the radial basis vectors plus a forward tilt, then orienting each card so it faces along that flattened flow direction relative to its surface normal.

Now I'm sketching the head paint logic using a per-pixel function based on local coordinates relative to the head center, applying a zigzag pattern along x to create a jagged boundary between cream and base fur color on the cheek/muzzle area, with plans to extend similar cream shading around the eyes.

Good, that region works for the brow patch. Now I'm adding a tear-stripe marking beneath the eye, defining a narrow diagonal band of deeper rust color that needs to be layered correctly against the cream region.

Setting up the default rust gradient fill for the rest of the face and ears, then adding cream tufted cards along the chest and neck ruff with a normal-vector filter to position them on the front-facing surfaces.

For the body, I'm layering rust and plum fur tufts via scatter patterns—upper body gets rust tufts with varied size and lean angle for a fluffy cel-shaded look, while the underbelly gets plum tufts filtered by downward-facing normals.

Now I'm working out the tail: positioning a gold band ring around the tail at a specific point along its length, calculating the tail's radius there by interpolating between keyframe values so the ring fits snugly with proper clearance, then checking that the fluff cards along the tail don't awkwardly clip through that ring.

I decide to delay the start of the tail tufts until further along so the band area stays clear, and figure out how to reference the correct bone joint for positioning. I also sketch a small hanging charm beneath the ring, oriented to dangle naturally given the tail's angle at that point, before moving on to adding a few more boulders to the stone assembly.

I'm scattering a handful of faceted boulder spheres and flattened moss caps around the base ring, tuning their scale, vertical offset, and angular placement so they peek out from the lathe stone without overlapping the front-facing decal.

Now I'm positioning the moss-card frames around the stone rim at radius 0.345, spacing 24 of them, then placing four glow flowers on the moss cap near the edge while avoiding the paw areas.

Writing flower petal spheres...

I'm deciding against adding floating seeds or motes since they'd violate the floor-contact/hang rules, keeping it simpler instead. I'll focus the glow motifs on the forehead gem, pendant, rune stone, and flowers, and consider whether the tail tip should glow too.

For small details, I'm thinking a tiny glowing charm could hang off a tassel ring at the tail like a leaf-bead accent, and settling on a gold leaf-fan ornament at the forehead with a glowing octahedron gem at its base. Writing paint functions for mossy and stone surfaces...

Checking the lowest points against total height ratio confirms the proportions stay within bounds, and the tail and ear heights also check out fine. The overall part count seems manageable.

Skipping extra accessories like a gold belt or cape—keeping it simple with a collar pendant and gold tail cuffs is enough for the Genshin-inspired look. The big anime eyes with teal iris are set, and I'm considering a small sphere for cream brow marks via paint handles.

Writing eye and skin decal code...

The decal direction is based on hit normal so the eyes face outward-forward correctly, and the eye bone weighting ties properly to the head. I'm double-checking paint/fill parameters and flat shading options for consistency across parts.

Now I'm working on the boulder geometry, applying stone paint with flat shading and positioning it on the hips bone, then setting up a lathe profile for the stone outline with typed point tuples to satisfy the geometry's expected coordinate format.

The lathe outline runs from the central axis outward and back, with explicit bottom and top points closing the shape along the axis—I'm checking that zero-x points don't cause rendering issues. Now I'm defining the moss cap profile as an array of coordinate pairs and starting a height function based on the x position for shaping the moss surface.

Writing the moss height lookup function...

I'm estimating how faceting the lathe with 12 segments slightly reduces radial extent, which should be negligible, and computing leg attachment points using the moss height function at specific front and hind positions to get consistent Y offsets for mounting.

Still defining leg joint coordinates...

Now I'm setting up the tail chain parented to hips, defining its path points starting inside the rump and tapering sweep radii, then writing a custom paint function for the tail coloring based on position.

Writing color logic for rust-to-plum gradient, using a zigzag pattern for banding and making sure the tip ends in dark plum to match red-panda coloring, then setting up alternating ring textures along the tail.

Now I'm placing individual tuft cards along the tail sweep, randomizing their angle and position while orienting each card's local axis to follow the tangent of the sweep frame.

For colors, I'm splitting tufts into rust/deep shade groups by parity, adding a plum tip near the tail's end, and picking a handpicked shadow shade for the rust tufts. Moving on to the body fluff, ruffs, pendant tassel bead, and whisker placement details.

Continuing the whiskers, I'm positioning three thin rods per side with slight vertical offsets in a cream-white tone, skipping teeth and tongue since the mouth stays closed, and now working out the mouth line and muzzle geometry to make sure the lip positions align with the muzzle sphere's surface.

Mouth ends around z .478, so I'll place the side points slightly outward using that value and keep the rods thin at radius 0.003 so they stay hidden against the surface. Actually, it might be simpler to skip the mouth line entirely rather than risk a visible seam.

I decide to keep it with a tiny offset for charm. I'm adding scattered cheek tuft cards leaning outward-back, a sprinkling of rust tufts between the ears filtered to the upper skull, and considering hind haunch spheres and a spine fur crest, though lighting orientation shouldn't matter here. I'm wary of complexity creeping in with the skull surface binding.

I'm checking that the surface and scatter helpers pass hit data correctly into the card system, that direction and point inputs accept plain array literals and nested arrays, and that frame and part positions can take Vector3 objects directly. I'm sketching hanging card frames with flipped orientation, skipping any extra scarf decoration, defining a quick vector constructor helper, and sketching a small gold ear stud using a torus and sphere positioned near the lower ear edge.

Still working out ear ornament placement...

Writing the TypeScript build function...

Laying out the build order: stone parts, body, legs and paws, head, tail, then gold accessories and moss decor. I'm defining a reusable leg-building function that takes side and front/back parameters to generate symmetric limb chains with proper joint hierarchy.

Setting up joint names for front legs (shoulder, elbow, wrist, paw) and hind legs (hip, knee, ankle, foot), each tagged with a "leg" role and a contact point under the foot for ground placement, then sweeping a tapered profile along each chain to form the limb geometry, with the tip joint used to attach the paw part.

Now I'm positioning toe spheres and claws at the front of each paw, then placing a gold bangle torus along the wrist-to-elbow direction on the front legs, followed by adding haunch and shoulder muscle blobs and setting the paw pad color.

I'm defining a shading function that picks coat colors based on surface normal and position—dark plum on the belly, deep rust along a dorsal stripe, and mottled rust elsewhere—but I realize calling the mottle function fresh for every texel is wasteful since it recreates a paint object each time, so I should hoist that out and reuse it.

Now I'm sketching paint functions for the legs, neck, and tail that mix cream, plum, and the precomputed rust mottle depending on normal and position, then setting up the muzzle as a small cream sphere attached to the head bone.

Precomputing the cel-shaded palette...

Adding the jaw sphere with cream color, then working on a gold forehead ornament by extruding a leaf-crown outline along the head's surface normal, making sure the points stay non-self-crossing.

Checking the short edge there—cutting corners at a quarter length along each neighboring edge still avoids crossings, so smoothing level 1 should be safe even near that notch. I'll keep smoothing at 1 but may need to mark the notch corners as sharp to preserve their shape.

Actually, to reduce risk I'll switch to smoothing 0 for a crisp, faceted look, using a tiny bevel of 0.0015 that shrinks automatically at sharp or concave corners. The leaf outline with 10 points works fine here with no sharp markings needed since smoothing is already 0.

Now I'm placing a small glowing gem at the base of the ornament, positioned using a helper that converts azimuth, elevation, and lift into a 3D point along the head's surface.

Still writing coordinate code...

For the eyebrow decals, moss flowers, and pendant placement I still need to work out the exact positions. For the collar, I'm computing a tangent point along the neck's curved path at roughly the midpoint, using the chain's interpolation and tangent direction to orient a torus piece, and binding it to the nearest neck joint for rigging purposes.

Now I'm working out the pendant's hanging position by projecting a downward vector perpendicular to the neck tangent, so it drapes naturally off the front-lower neck, then sizing and positioning it so the ruff collar's tufts don't completely obscure it -- possibly enlarging the gem or filtering which ruff cards get placed near that spot.

Defining pendant frame and gem geometry...

I'll keep the collar simple with a torus and skip extra beads, and set head spheres to low-poly 12x8. Then I'm placing the boulders, mossy patches, and a ring of hanging moss cards around the figure.

For the moss cards I'm making each one face radially outward from the center so they're visible from all sides, using an angle-based flow function. For the grass on the cap, I'm varying the lean and using a golden-angle rotation per blade so growth directions look naturally randomized.

Now I'm working out flower placement on the cap, checking coordinates against the paw positions so flowers don't overlap them, adjusting radius and height values to keep everything spaced sensibly.

I'm checking that the decal placement on the stone's lathe surface roughly aligns near y=0.12, accounting for the faceting from the 12 segments which might shift the actual surface point slightly from the nominal radius.

For the side decals, I'm confirming the position and direction vectors point outward correctly, and that materials cloned for decals work fine with the alphaTest texture setup. I'm also noting which utility functions (noise, cells, patches, mottle, paint, catmull) I'll need for painting cracks and details on the stone, then moving to write the final code.

For the stone surface, I'm defining a cracked-rock paint function: using cell noise to detect crack borders, adding wobble noise to blend moss patches onto upward-facing surfaces, and falling back to plain rock texture otherwise, making sure cracks render under moss so they stay visible only on bare rock. I'll reuse this same paint function for the boulder decorations, just at different positions.

Now I'm defining the fluff tuft color palettes (rust, cream, plum, grass tones) before moving to ear geometry. For the ears, I'm computing a basis per side using the aim direction and an up vector to get perpendicular axes, then placing a small scaled sphere on the head bone oriented along that direction, checking that the mirrored side produces a correctly flipped but consistent orientation.

Writing rim tuft placement...

I'm positioning the rim tufts around the ear's edge using the perpendicular basis vectors and angle sweeps, adding card-based fluff texture along the outer curve, inner ear shading, and a small gold bead accent at the ear tip, then moving on to eye detailing next.

Skipping that, I'll return the finished bone root and verify the loft and chain configurations — checking that joint references resolve correctly, the hips-spine bone ordering matches their z-positions along the spine, and that the body path spans correctly from the rump through the neck and chest regions.

Now I'm confirming the tail card sweep uses the right angle and lift parameters, and sketching out typed arrays for the mirrored side coordinates to keep TypeScript strictness happy.

I'm double-checking frame direction vectors, part tagging, and the SVG texture setup, then settling on the flat color palette and finishing the flower petal geometry before writing out the final file.
